notes: First challenge to post-2003 discretionary leave policy; Gibbs J refused JR and permission to appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Shahid: judicial review of three-year discretionary leave after Article 8 success
key_facts: Mr Shahid, a Pakistani national, had lived in the United Kingdom for about ten years after his asylum claim was mishandled and eventually succeeded on Article 8 before an adjudicator in April 2003.
Following that success the Secretary of State granted three years' discretionary leave rather than indefinite leave to remain, applying the new April 2003 policy on leave outside the Rules.
The claimant argued that indefinite leave was required to respect his established private and family life and that limited leave left him in unacceptable uncertainty.
Maurice Kay LJ granted permission to apply for judicial review, but the Home Office later filed evidence showing the decision had properly considered the policy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of discretionary leave decisions after an Article 8 immigration appeal; permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal refused at the end of the hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review refused; application for permission to appeal refused; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where removal would breach Article 8, granting discretionary leave for three years under the Secretary of State's published policy is a rational exercise of discretion and does not itself infringe Article 8; limited leave does not prevent social integration and the policy presumptively leads to settlement after six years absent material change.
legal_issues: Whether refusal of indefinite leave was Wednesbury irrational or applied the policy inflexibly
Whether limited discretionary leave itself breached Article 8 as a positive obligation
Whether the court should apply heightened scrutiny to immigration policy decisions
Construction of the April 2003 discretionary leave and settlement policy
linked_authorities: R (Razgar) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 27
R (Anufrijeva) v Southwark London Borough Council [2003] UKHL 36

confidence.notes: Policy analysis, Article 8 reasoning and final disposal are clearly recorded; described as the first reported challenge to the new discretionary leave policy.

notes: Birth injury appeal; IUGR error acknowledged but negligence finding upheld on detailed factual review.

enrichment.short_title: Morris v Blackpool Hospital: cerebral palsy appeal after IUGR finding error
key_facts: Christopher Morris was born in June 1987 with severe cerebral palsy after intra-uterine growth retardation and alleged hypoxic ischaemic brain damage in the womb.
Silber J dismissed the claim at trial on preliminary issues, finding no negligence in failing to scan on 19/20 May 1987 and rejecting in utero causation.
On appeal it was common ground that the judge erred in finding Christopher did not suffer IUGR, but the hospital maintained other findings survived.
The claim had narrowed to whether antenatal signs on 19/20 May 1987 should have triggered ultrasound scanning and earlier delivery.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a trial on preliminary issues of breach and causation in a clinical negligence claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge's finding of no negligence on 19/20 May 1987 was upheld despite his error on the IUGR diagnosis.
enrichment.ratio: A trial judge's erroneous finding that a baby did not suffer pathological IUGR does not undermine a separately reasoned finding of no breach where fundal height and maternal weight gave no suspicious indication for scanning; causation on treatment and timing would also have remained difficult even if negligence had been established.
legal_issues: Effect of the judge's IUGR error on liability and causation findings
Whether antenatal fundal height and weight measurements required scanning for IUGR
Bolam and Bolitho standard for obstetric management on 19/20 May 1987
Whether in utero hypoxic ischaemia or postnatal polycythaemia caused the brain damage
linked_authorities: Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee [1957] 1 WLR 582
Bolitho v City and Hackney Health Authority [1998] AC 232
Wilsher v Essex Area Health Authority [1988] AC 1074

confidence.notes: Complex medical evidence but appellate conclusions on negligence and the limited effect of the IUGR error are explicit.

notes: Split Court of Appeal on breach; choice of law analysis for Guernsey director duties is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Base Metal v Shamurin: choice of law and director's duty over LME speculation
key_facts: Base Metal Trading Ltd, a Guernsey company controlled by Russian directors, traded metals and hedged on the London Metal Exchange through managing director Mr Shamurin from Moscow.
After a falling out, BMTL sued Shamurin for speculative LME losses of over $6m beyond the agreed hedging policy.
Tomlinson J held Russian law governed the tort and equitable claims and that no breach was established even on English/Guernsey law.
The Court of Appeal upheld Russian law for tort but held Guernsey law governed the equitable duty of care as a matter of company constitution.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Commercial Court trial on choice of law and breach of duty in director/employee LME trading claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed by the majority; Russian law applied to tort, Guernsey law to equity, but no breach of duty was established on the facts.
enrichment.ratio: A director's equitable duty of care to a company is governed by the law of the place of incorporation, not the law governing a related employment contract; concurrent contract and tort claims may attract different proper laws, and speculative trading beyond an agreed hedging policy is not necessarily a breach where the managing director had authority to trade futures.
legal_issues: Proper law of tort, contract and equitable director duties under the Rome Convention
Whether double actionability should be displaced for Russian-connected conduct
Whether Shamurin had authority to enter speculative LME trades
Whether tort and equitable duties are contractual obligations for Rome Convention purposes
linked_authorities: Coupland v Arabian Gulf Oil Co [1983] 1 WLR 1136
Bristol and West Building Society v Mothew [1998] Ch 1
Attorney General for England and Wales v R [2002] 2 NZLR 91

confidence.notes: Choice of law holdings are clear; breach outcome rests on a split court with Arden LJ dissenting on liability.

notes: Landlord and Tenant Act 1995 section 25 anti-avoidance; BHP distinguished on personal covenants.

enrichment.short_title: Avonridge v sublessees: void clause limiting lessor liability on assignment
key_facts: Avonridge granted long subleases of restaurant premises at Headstone Drive, Wealdstone, covenanting to pay the headlease rent but excluding its own liability after disposing of the reversion.
After assigning the headlease to Mr Phithwa, Avonridge remained named as landlord under the subleases when the headlessors forfeited for rent arrears.
Subtenants sought damages for breach of the rent covenant and argued the limiting words in clause 6 were void under section 25 of the 1995 Act.
The county court judge held the clause was an impermissible advance release from landlord covenants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from county court Part 20 proceedings for damages after relief against forfeiture of a headlease.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the clause limiting Avonridge's liability on assignment was void and Avonridge remained liable on the landlord covenants.
enrichment.ratio: A covenant binding successors in title but purporting to end the original lessor's liability on assignment is a landlord covenant within the 1995 Act, not a personal covenant; such an advance opt-out frustrates the section 8 release procedure and is void under section 25(1).
legal_issues: Whether the clause created a personal or landlord covenant
Application of section 25 anti-avoidance to pre-agreed termination of lessor liability
Distinction from personal covenants upheld in BHP Petroleum v Chesterfield Properties
Whether section 28(1) modified the definition of landlord covenant
linked_authorities: BHP Petroleum Great Britain Ltd v Chesterfield Properties Ltd [2002] Ch 194

confidence.notes: Statutory issue and dismissal are clearly reasoned with full Law Commission background.

notes: CPR 3.5 strike-out construction left open; appeal dismissed on case management discretion.

enrichment.short_title: Richardson v Langtree: whether non-disclosure order struck out the claim
key_facts: Langtree obtained judgment against Mr Richardson after trial on personal lease and guarantee liability totalling about £22,000.
Richardson argued a unless order of 19 September 2003 had struck out Langtree's claim when standard disclosure was not fully complied with by 1 October 2003.
A disclosure list was served on 30 September and a signed list on 6 October; Richardson continued preparing for trial and pressed for copy documents.
On the first day of trial HHJ Taylor allowed the claim to proceed despite Richardson's strike-out application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission on whether the action had been automatically struck out before trial for disclosure non-compliance.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge was entitled to refuse to treat the claim as struck out and to proceed to trial.
enrichment.ratio: Even if a unless order threatened strike-out for disclosure default, a court hearing the matter after partial compliance and extensive trial preparation may properly exercise its discretion under the overriding objective to let the claim proceed where the defendant suffered no prejudice from late service of the disclosure statement.
legal_issues: Construction of CPR 3.5 where an unless order says the claim will be struck out without further order
Whether Langtree complied with standard disclosure by serving lists and a signed statement
Exercise of discretion under CPR 3.9 when applying sanctions on the trial date
Whether the defendant was prejudiced by delayed disclosure

confidence.notes: Disposal rests on discretion rather than a final ruling on CPR 3.5 construction, which the court expressly left open.

notes: Sri Lankan asylum appeal; IAT reasoning inadequate and case remitted for rehearing.

enrichment.short_title: Nirmalanathan: Sri Lankan Tamil asylum appeal restored for inadequate IAT reasons
key_facts: Mr Nirmalanathan, a Sri Lankan Tamil, claimed asylum based on past LTTE support and fear of both the authorities and the LTTE.
An adjudicator found his father's killing by the army and continued army interest made his case exceptional despite the 2002 ceasefire.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal allowed the Secretary of State's appeal, criticising reliance on Dr Good's report and downplaying the factual basis of the claim.
Laws LJ granted permission to appeal, doubting the Tribunal had properly reasoned its reversal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal challenge to an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision restoring a refused asylum claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the Tribunal's decision set aside and the case remitted for rehearing rather than restoring the adjudicator outright.
enrichment.ratio: An immigration tribunal must give properly reasoned decisions explaining why it departs from an adjudicator's findings; it cannot set aside a credible fact-sensitive asylum assessment by misstating the evidence base or ignoring country guidance such as Jeyachandran without adequate analysis.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT mischaracterised the adjudicator's reliance on Dr Good and Jeyachandran
Risk on return to Sri Lanka for a Tamil with LTTE links after the ceasefire
When the Court of Appeal should remit rather than restore an adjudicator's decision
Exceptionality under country guidance determinations
linked_authorities: Jeyachandran v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] UKIAT 01869

confidence.notes: Appellate criticism of Tribunal reasoning is detailed; remittal rather than final restoration leaves merits partly open.

notes: TCC trial on contracting party and Sale of Goods Act fitness of floor tiles.

enrichment.short_title: Area Solutions v Tasty Wok: slip-resistant tile breach and contracting party
key_facts: Refurbishment work was carried out for a new Chinese buffet restaurant at Solihull Ice Rink trading as Wok's Hall.
Norwood/Area Solutions supplied and laid Milleto Verde restaurant tiles and Wooliscroft kitchen tiles said to be non-slip Grade 5.
Mr Chan personally dealt with the contractor while Tasty Wok Ltd was later incorporated; unpaid invoices exceeded £31,500.
Expert evidence showed R9 tiles were below DIN and Tile Association guidance for wet commercial restaurant and kitchen use.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial on liability for unpaid invoices and a set-off counterclaim for defective flooring.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for the claimant subject to a £9,034 set-off for supplying tiles not reasonably fit for purpose; net recovery about £22,500.
enrichment.ratio: Where quotations and payments were made with Mr Chan personally before objectively clear corporate adoption, contracts were with him rather than Tasty Wok Ltd; tiles supplied for a commercial restaurant knowing non-slip use was required breached section 14(3) if their R rating fell below accepted industry standards.
legal_issues: Whether the contractor contracted with Mr Chan or Tasty Wok Limited
Fitness for purpose of Grade 5 tiles under section 14(3)
Applicable R rating standards for kitchen and restaurant floors
Measure of damages for overlaying replacement slip-resistant tiles

confidence.notes: Findings on identity of contracting party and tile fitness are explicit with agreed figures for judgment and set-off.

notes: Quantum-only appeal on discretionary bonus damages; partial reduction and remittal for redetermination.

enrichment.short_title: Cantor Fitzgerald v Horkulak: discretionary bonus damages after wrongful dismissal
key_facts: Steven Horkulak, a senior interest-rate derivatives manager at Cantor Fitzgerald, was wrongfully dismissed during a fixed-term contract paying £250,000 basic salary plus discretionary bonus.
Newman J awarded about £892,000, largely for lost discretionary bonuses he held would rationally have been paid had Horkulak completed the term.
Cantor Fitzgerald appealed on quantum only, arguing a purely discretionary bonus clause could not support such an award.
The Court of Appeal reduced the award by £116,667 for mitigation and earnings credit and referred quantum back to the trial judge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal on damages only after liability for wrongful dismissal was upheld.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal partly allowed in amount; damages reduced by £116,667; issue of discretionary bonus quantum remitted to Newman J for redetermination on existing evidence.
enrichment.ratio: A contractual discretionary bonus clause does not exclude damages for wrongful dismissal, but assessment requires the court to ask what bonus rational decision-makers would have paid applying stated criteria; inadequate judicial reasoning on quantum may require redetermination rather than full retrial, and mitigation loss may be reduced where relapse was not attributable to the employer.
legal_issues: Recoverability of lost discretionary bonus after wrongful dismissal
Application of Lavarack v Woods and Clark v Nomura to bonus clauses
Assessment of likely bonus level using employer criteria
Mitigation and credit for earnings during psychiatric relapse
linked_authorities: Lavarack v Woods of Colchester Ltd [1967] 1 QB 278
Clark v Nomura International plc [2000] IRLR 766
English v Emery Reimbold & Strick Ltd [2002] EWCA Civ 605

confidence.notes: Detailed quantum reasoning though final order was deferred pending a further hearing on remittal terms.

notes: Case stated on Protection from Harassment Act course of conduct; magistrates' findings upheld.

enrichment.short_title: A v DPP: harassment conviction upheld for threats to burn victim's home
key_facts: The appellant repeatedly visited and abused Kimberley Harris at her home between June and December 2003, demanding money and threatening to burn the house and damage property.
He smashed a car window in her presence in November 2003 and continued abusive visits after a period in custody.
Magistrates convicted him under section 4 for a course of conduct causing fear of violence, finding fear on at least two occasions when he threatened arson.
Miss Harris gave evidence she felt threatened throughout the period even if not unduly concerned on the first arson threat.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by way of case stated from Oxfordshire magistrates' conviction for harassment causing fear of violence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the magistrates' findings that the victim feared violence on at least two occasions were supported by the evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Threats to burn down the house where the victim lives can amount to threats of violence against her for section 4 purposes; a course of conduct is established where fear of violence is caused on at least two occasions, and magistrates may properly find fear existed throughout intimidation even if the victim also described herself as not unduly concerned on one occasion.
legal_issues: Whether threats against property amounted to fear of violence against the victim
Need for at least two occasions causing fear forming a course of conduct
Effect of threats directed mainly at third parties under Curtin v DPP
Whether magistrates could rely on later fear relating back to an earlier threat
linked_authorities: Curtin v Director of Public Prosecutions [2002] EWHC Admin 971

confidence.notes: Short case stated appeal with clear affirmative answer to the magistrates' principal question.

notes: Section 51 intimidation appeal; court refined meaning of intimidate but upheld conviction.

enrichment.short_title: Patrascu: meaning of intimidating a witness under section 51

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Mr Patrascu was convicted of intimidating witness Philip Chapman before a magistrates' court trial for begging.
Outside court he pursued Chapman, leaned on his shoulder, shouted in his ear and pressed him to lie that they knew each other.
Chapman said the behaviour was intimidating but that he was not intimidated, though he was annoyed and concerned about meeting Patrascu again.
The recorder directed the jury that pressure short of fear could suffice; Patrascu received six months consecutive to another sentence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction with leave on the construction and sufficiency of evidence for section 51(1) witness intimidation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction safe despite imperfect direction because the evidence supported intimidation by threat and aggressive conduct.
enrichment.ratio: Section 51(1) requires an act which intimidates, intended to intimidate, with knowledge the victim is a witness and intent to obstruct justice; intimidation includes putting the victim in fear or seeking to deter by threat or violence, and the victim need not actually feel intimidated if the defendant's conduct was threatening, though mere pressure without threat or fear is insufficient.
legal_issues: Whether the victim must have felt intimidated for a section 51 conviction
Construction of 'an act which intimidates' beyond putting someone in fear
Whether pressure to change evidence alone suffices
Sufficiency of evidence where the witness denied feeling intimidated
catchwords: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and safe-conviction analysis are clearly articulated despite partial misdirection on pressure alone.
